'''''Amaranthus spinosus''''', commonly known as the '''spiny amaranth''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=AMSP|taxon=Amaranthus spinosusaccessdate=7 January 2016}}</ref> '''spiny pigweed''', '''prickly amaranth''' or '''thorny amaranth''', is a plant that is native to the tropical Americas, but is present on most continents as an [[introduced species]] and sometimes a [[noxious weed]].{{citation needed|date=August 2022}} It can be a serious weed of [[rice]] cultivation in [[Asia]].<ref>{{cite book|title=A practical field guide to weeds of rice in Asia |author=Caton, B. P. |author2=M. Mortimer |author3=J. E. Hill  |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ver3qCQF9EEC&q=field+guide |year=2004 |pages=20–21 |publisher=International Rice Research Institute |isbn=9789712201912 }}</ref>

== Description ==
''Amaranthus spinosus'' is a vascular flowering plant in the [[Dicotyledon|dicot]] family [[Amaranthaceae]]. As described in the species name, ''A. spinosus'' has spikes present on the flowers and spines present at nodes. The flowers are green, lack petals, and have terminal and axillary spikes. Male flowers are terminal while the female flowers are basal. The ovate or rhombic-ovate leaves are alternate with long petioles.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Taylor |first=Walter Kingsley |title=The Guide to Florida Wildflowers |publisher=Taylor Trade Publishing |year=1992}}</ref>

==Uses==
===Dye use===
In [[Khmer language]], it is called ''pti banlar'' and in [[Vietnamese language|Vietnamese]] {{lang|vi|dền}} and its ash was historically used as a grey [[dye|cloth dye]].

===Food use===
[[File:Phat phak khom.jpg|thumb|''Phat phak khom'' is a Thai stir-fried dish of the young [[Shoot (botany)|shoot]]s of the ''Amaranthus spinosus''. This version is stir-fried with egg and minced pork.]]
Like several related species, ''A. spinosus'' is a valued food plant in Africa. In southern Mozambique is called mboa and is food for both humans and some mammals<ref name="prota">Grubben, G.J.H. & Denton, O.A. (2004) Plant Resources of Tropical Africa 2. Vegetables. PROTA Foundation, Wageningen; Backhuys, Leiden; CTA, Wageningen.</ref> In Brazil it is known as "caruru de porco", being used pure braised or added to salty porridge preparations, such as [[angu]] (<small>[[:pt:Angu|pt]]</small>) and is more common in the interior regions of the country. It is valued also in [[Thai cuisine]], where it is called ''phak khom'' ({{langx|th|ผักขม}}). In Tamil, it is called ''mullik keerai''. It is possible identical to Sanskrit ''taṇḍulīyaka''. It is used as food in the [[Philippines]], where it is called ''kulitis''. The leaves of this plant, known as ''massaagu'' in the [[Maldivian language]], have been used in the diet of the [[Maldives]].<ref>[[Xavier Romero-Frias]], ''The Maldive Islanders, A Study of the Popular Culture of an Ancient Ocean Kingdom.'' Barcelona 1999, {{ISBN|84-7254-801-5}}</ref>  In Mexico, it is among the species labelled ''quelite quintonil'' in Mexican markets.
In Bengali it is called ''katanote'' (কাটানটে). In Manipuri, it is called ''chengkrook'' and is used as food in stir-fry and in broths mixed with other vegetables.
In Mauritius it is called ''brède malbar''.
The seeds are eaten by many songbirds.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-year=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=320}}</ref>

===Traditional medicine===
In the [[Traditional medicine|folk medicine]] of [[India]], the ash of fruits of ''Amaranthus spinosus'' is used for [[jaundice]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.3389/fphar.2017.00518| title = Ethnopharmacological Approaches for Therapy of Jaundice: Part I| journal = Frontiers in Pharmacology| volume = 8| year = 2017| last1 = Tewari| first1 = Devesh| last2 = Mocan| first2 = Andrei| last3 = Parvanov| first3 = Emil D| last4 = Sah| first4 = Archana N| last5 = Nabavi| first5 = Seyed M| last6 = Huminiecki| first6 = Lukasz| last7 = Ma| first7 = Zheng Feei| last8 = Lee| first8 = Yeong Yeh| last9 = Horbańczuk| first9 = Jarosław O| last10 = Atanasov| first10 = Atanas G| page = 518| pmc = 5559545| pmid=28860989| doi-access = free}}</ref>{{medical citation needed|date=June 2018}}  Water extracts from its roots and leaves have been used as a diuretic in Vietnam.<ref>{{ cite book | first1=Yoshitaka | last1=Tanaka | first2=Nguyen | last2=Van Ke | date=2007 | title=Edible Wild Plants of Vietnam: The Bountiful Garden | publisher=Thailand: Orchid Press | isbn=978-9745240896 | page=22}}</ref>{{medical citation needed|date=May 2017}}
